title: The three-sentence answer
goal: Answer a question about a news report in three sentences: answer, evidence, explain.

card.title: A – E – E: ANSWER · EVIDENCE · EXPLAIN
lines: A: ANSWER the question in one full sentence. Use the question's words.
E: EVIDENCE. Write 'The report says…' and add the detail. You may copy its words.
E: EXPLAIN. Write 'This shows…' and say what the detail proves.
Does the question ask two things? Answer both in your A sentence.
Check: Did I answer every part? Is it under 100 words?

T.label: true, but not what they asked
T.feedback: It is in the report, but it answers a different question.

N.label: not from the report
N.feedback: That is not in the report. Evidence has to come from the report.

R.label: repeats the answer
R.feedback: That says the answer again. It does not say what the evidence proves.

X.label: does not connect
X.feedback: That does not connect the evidence to the answer.

F.label: not a full answer
F.feedback: That is only a piece. It does not answer the question in a full sentence.

P.label: missed a part
P.feedback: Look for AND joining two questions. Count the parts again.

levels.description: Answer, evidence and explanation are all there, and every part of the question is answered.
Two of the three (for example, a correct answer with evidence but no explanation), or all three with one part of the question missing.
Nothing usable: off topic, or only copied text with no answer.
Says what the evidence proves and links it to the answer.
Repeats the answer or the evidence in other words.

bike.title: Teens Build Free Bike Repair Stand Outside Library
sentences: WESTVIEW — A group of Grade 10 students has installed a free bike repair stand outside the Westview Public Library, and it has been busy since the day it opened.
The stand, bolted to the sidewalk near the bike racks, holds a pump, wrenches, screwdrivers and tire levers on steel cables.

The students built it as a project for their technology class after noticing that many classmates rode bikes with flat tires or loose brakes because the nearest repair shop is a 40-minute bus ride away.
"We fixed about fifteen bikes in the first week, and then people started fixing their own," said Aisha Rahman, 15, one of the builders.
The library paid for the materials, about $600, from its community fund.
Librarian Tom Reyes said the stand has brought new visitors inside: "People come to fix a tire and leave with a library card."
The students plan to add a laminated guide showing how to patch a tube.
They hope another school will copy the idea next year.

quiet.title: School Opens Quiet Room for Students Who Need a Break
sentences: MAPLEWOOD — Maplewood Secondary opened a "quiet room" on Monday, a former storage room on the second floor with dim lights, two beanbag chairs and no screens.
Students can use the room for up to fifteen minutes during class time if a teacher gives them a pass.
Guidance counsellor Priya Nair said the room was created after a survey last spring in which 40 percent of students said they sometimes felt too overwhelmed to stay in class.
"Before, the only options were the hallway or the office, and neither one is calming," Nair said.
In the first week, the room was used 62 times.
Grade 11 student Devon Clarke said he used it before a presentation.
"Ten minutes with no noise and I could breathe again," he said.
Some teachers worried students would use the room to skip class, so passes are recorded and the room is checked every fifteen minutes.
Nair said the school will look at the numbers in December to decide whether to keep the room.

desk.title: Students Run a Free Tech Help Desk for Seniors
sentences: EASTGATE — Every Wednesday after school, six students from Eastgate Collegiate set up a table in the Eastgate Seniors' Centre and wait for questions.
The students help older adults with their phones and tablets, from sending photos to booking a doctor's appointment online.
Teacher Mark Bell started the help desk in January after his own grandmother missed an appointment because she could not open an email.
"Many seniors are embarrassed to ask their families again and again," Bell said.
About twenty seniors now come each week, and some bring a written list of questions.
Volunteer Jaya Menon, 16, said the hardest part is slowing down.
"I had to learn to let them tap the screen themselves, even when it takes longer," she said.
The centre's director, Helen Park, said several seniors have started video calling their grandchildren for the first time.
The students earn volunteer hours for their work, and the program will continue until June.
desk.tutorNote: Eastgate and the people in this report are invented.

arena.title: Arena Offers Free Friday Skating for Teens
sentences: NORTHBROOK — The Northbrook Arena is now free for teenagers on Friday nights from 7 to 9 p.m.
The town council started the program in November after police reported groups of teens gathering in the plaza parking lot with nothing to do.
Skate rentals are free too, thanks to forty pairs donated by a local sports store.
About ninety teens came on the first Friday, more than the arena expected.
"We ran out of size nine skates in ten minutes," said arena manager Paul Demers.
Some neighbours on Birch Street, beside the front entrance, complained about noise when the crowd left at nine o'clock.
In response, the arena now closes its front doors at the end of the night and sends everyone out the back exit, which opens onto the main road.
Grade 10 student Maria Lopez said she comes every week.
"It's the one night all my friends are in the same place," she said.
Council will vote in March on whether to keep the program next winter.
arena.tutorNote: Northbrook and the people in this report are invented.

sections.title: Three sentences
sections.tutorNote: I DO. Read the three sentences on the card. Look at the news report together: the headline, the place in capitals, the first lines (who, what, where, when), the quotation marks. Reveal the worked example one step at a time, thinking aloud. Then sort the six sentences: which is the answer, which is evidence, which explains?

text: Some questions ask you to write about a news report.
Answer in three sentences. Do this every time.
A: ANSWER the question in one full sentence. Use the question's words.
E: EVIDENCE. Write 'The report says…' and add the detail. You may copy its words.
E: EXPLAIN. Write 'This shows…' and say what the detail proves.
Does the question ask two things? Answer both in your A sentence.
This is a news report.
The first word is in capitals. It names the place.
The first sentences tell who, what, where and when.
Words in quotation marks are what a person said.
The end often tells what will happen next.

sections.title: Build one together
sections.tutorNote: WE DO. For the first question the student finds the proof, then chooses the answer, the evidence and the explanation one at a time; read each wrong choice aloud and say why it fails. The second question has two parts, and its second part needs an inference: the A sentence answers both parts, and the evidence comes from what Aisha Rahman said. The student says each sentence aloud before typing it. (The model answers here follow the three boxes exactly, so some are worded differently from the paper guide.)

sections.title: The sentence people skip
sections.tutorNote: WE DO. The Explain sentence is the one that gets skipped, and it is what separates a middle score from a top one. Each screen gives the answer and the evidence; the student chooses, then writes, only the explanation. Ask: what does that detail PROVE? If the student repeats the answer, say 'That is your answer again.' The typed ones go to the review queue; score 0 to 2.

text: People often skip the third sentence.
It does not repeat your answer.
It says what the evidence PROVES.
Start it with 'This shows…'.

sections.title: Write one on your own
sections.tutorNote: YOU DO on a new report. The question has two parts. The student taps the proof first, then writes in three boxes with the sentence starters. It goes to the review queue; score 0 to 3, and note parts answered, evidence specific, explanation linked and the word count. As a rough guide only, in the test's own codes: all three with both parts is about a 30; a missing explanation or a missing part about a 20; one vague point about a 10.
